definition.text: The particular set of environmental conditions and the role that a species or population occupies in its surroundings.

facts.text: The word was coined in 1910 by Roswell Hill Johnson, and Joseph Grinnell first used it in ecological research in 1917.
Grinnell's niche is set by the habitat a species lives in and the behaviours that let it persist and reproduce there.
In 1927 Charles Elton defined a niche by an animal's place in the living environment, especially its relations to food and enemies.
A niche can be described along many axes, including life history, habitat, position in the food chain and geographic range.
Once a niche is left empty, other organisms can fill it; introduced species may invade the niches of native organisms and outcompete them.
Every species evolved for a certain niche, so climate change, by shifting temperature and weather, puts species at risk.

definition.text: A view of the niche as a many-dimensional space whose axes are the conditions and resources a species needs for its population to persist.

facts.text: The zoologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson popularized this niche concept in 1957, asking why so many kinds of organisms live in one habitat.
His work led to ideas such as niche breadth, the variety of resources or habitats a species uses.
Turning a species' fundamental niche into a map of where it could live is the task of niche modelling.

definition.text: The fundamental niche is the full range of conditions a species could use without other species interfering; the realized niche is the narrower part it actually occupies.

facts.text: Pressure from other species, especially competition, usually squeezes a species into a narrower realized niche.
For example, a species able to live on a whole hillside may hold only its top because a stronger competitor excludes it lower down.
Similarly, a species' realized geographic range is a narrower subset of its fundamental range, limited by other species or barriers.

definition.text: The process by which competing species use their environment in different ways, which helps them live side by side.

facts.text: It is also called niche segregation, niche separation or niche partitioning.
Species that differentiate their niches compete less strongly and are more likely to coexist.
Resource partitioning is one form: some lizard species seem to coexist by eating insects of different sizes.
Differentiation can come from current competition, from past extinction of weaker competitors, or from species evolving different patterns of resource use.
Some species, such as a group of hispine beetles, share the same food and habitat with no evidence of niche differentiation.
Different plants living together can play complementary roles such as nutrient cycling and water regulation, a mechanism called niche complementarity.

definition.text: The rule that two species competing for the same limited resource cannot both persist at steady numbers.

facts.text: It is sometimes called Gause's law and summed up as 'complete competitors cannot coexist'.
A species with even a slight advantage dominates in the long run, so the weaker competitor dies out or shifts to a different niche.
Invasive species can drive native species locally extinct through competitive exclusion.
Ecologists Andrewartha and Birch argued that most natural populations rarely exhaust their resources, so too much weight on competition is wrong.

definition.text: The variety of ecosystems found within a region or across the whole planet.

facts.text: It covers both living features and non-living ones such as water and soil, and includes land and water ecosystems.
Globally it spans deserts, forests, grasslands, wetlands and oceans, and it is the largest scale of biodiversity.
Diverse ecosystems help supply oxygen, purify water and provide plants used as medicines.
Crop-pollinating insects are worth $14.6 billion a year to the US economy, and hand pollination would cost $5,715-$7,135 more per hectare.

definition.text: The study of how the living and non-living parts of an ecosystem interact as one integrated system.

facts.text: It focuses on functional processes such as primary production, decomposition and feeding relationships that keep ecosystems and their services going.
Eugene Odum and Howard T. Odum quantified flows of energy and matter through whole ecosystems.
Its findings have improved sustainable production of forage, fibre, fuel and water.
Most natural ecosystems are limited by nitrogen, and recycling of nutrients, mainly from decomposing plant litter, keeps them productive.
Intensive fertilizer use in the US Midwest has degraded fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico, showing that maximizing output can harm ecosystem processes.
In Guatemala's western highlands, forest loss has raised landslide and water-shortage risks, while Totonicapán, which kept its forests, is more economically stable.

definition.text: The two ways an ecosystem's structure is shaped: from below by how much energy plants bring in, and from above by predators.

facts.text: Trophic dynamics is the transfer of energy and nutrients between organisms.
Energy captured by plants passes to herbivores, then carnivores, then top carnivores, and the total energy shrinks at each higher level.
Predators can dramatically shift which species dominate on land and at sea; the balance of the two controls is a major research question.
Herbivory can speed litter decomposition and nutrient cycling by changing litter quality and vegetation.
